findings.paper_title: Denbighshire County Council - Audit of Accounts report 2023-24 App 3
findings.headline: The auditor concludes that the going concern basis of accounting is appropriate and has identified no material uncertainties about the council's ability to continue.
findings.detail: This conclusion is made in the proposed audit report alongside the intended qualified opinion on the revaluation reserve and capital adjustment account. The paper states the going concern conclusion separately from that qualification.
findings.matters: A going concern conclusion without material uncertainty is the audit finding a lender is most likely to rely on, and it sits alongside the qualification in the same report.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.
findings.quote: In auditing the financial statements, I have concluded that the use of the going concern basis of accounting in the preparation of the financial statements is appropriate.

findings.paper_title: Denbighshire County Council - Audit of Accounts report 2023-24 App 3
findings.headline: The auditor has made seven recommendations, three of which were brought forward from the 2022-23 audit.
findings.detail: The recommendations cover capital accounting and valuation, reconciliation of populations, related parties, asset valuation approach, Section 106 agreements, leases and the quality of draft statements. Priority is high for six of the seven, with the Section 106 recommendation rated medium.
findings.matters: Recommendations carried over from one year to the next are a measure of how many audit issues remain open, which finance directors at peer councils can use for comparison.
findings.figures: Seven recommendations, of which three were brought forward from 2022-23.
findings.quote: We include seven recommendations as a result of our work, which includes three recommendations brought forward from our 2022-23 audit of accounts report.

findings.paper_title: Denbighshire County Council - Audit of Accounts report 2023-24 App 3
findings.headline: Two elected members failed to declare interests in two organisations, and transactions with both organisations needed to be added to the related party disclosures in Note 32.
findings.detail: Recommendation 3 describes the same issue as one elected member failing to declare a directorship in two organisations, so the paper gives different counts in different places. The council's management response says declarations for 2024-25 and 2025-26 have already been completed.
findings.matters: Completeness of member declarations is a control that finance directors and lenders look at when assessing governance, and the paper shows it was found incomplete.
findings.figures: Two elected members; two organisations; one elected member in the Appendix 5 version.
findings.quote: Two elected members had failed to declare their interests in two separate organisations.

findings.paper_title: Denbighshire County Council - Audit of Accounts report 2023-24 App 3
findings.headline: The council accepts that its draft financial statements for 2022-23 and 2023-24 do not meet the required standards, and a group is to be set up by the end of the calendar year to address the issues.
findings.detail: The management response describes a group of key officers from different disciplines to develop an action plan, with progress reported to the Head of Finance and Audit, CET and GAC. The 2024-25 accounts are the first to be prepared on the new finance system.
findings.matters: Acceptance of poor draft quality, and a new finance system in the first year of IFRS 16, are the reasons finance directors at other councils would give for their own accounts timetables.
findings.figures: Group to be set up by the end of the calendar year; new financial system from 1 April 2024.
findings.quote: The Council accepts that the quality of the draft financial statements for 2022-23 and 2023-24 does not meet the required standards.

findings.paper_title: Denbighshire County Council - Audit of Accounts report 2023-24 App 3
findings.headline: The auditor reports that the residual risk of material misstatement in asset valuations is low, after corrections to the financial statements.
findings.detail: Testing found errors in valuation inputs and missing source data for agricultural land, and the auditor says corrections were made in the statements. The paper says the residual risk across the population is low.
findings.matters: Valuation method and source data are the basis for the asset values lenders and finance directors use, and this paper shows both the errors found and the corrections made.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.
findings.quote: Our work has confirmed that the residual risk of material misstatement across the population is low.

findings.paper_title: Denbighshire County Council - Audit of Accounts report 2023-24 App 3
findings.headline: Lease registers were found to be incomplete and inconsistent, and the lease disclosures in Note 34 needed substantial amendments before they complied with the CIPFA Code.
findings.detail: The auditor found that supporting documentation was not available for some lease arrangements, including the determination of future lease periods. The auditor says the residual risk of material misstatement in Note 34 is now low.
findings.matters: Lease register quality is the input to the IFRS 16 balance sheet from 2024-25, so finance directors at other councils will look at their own registers in the same light.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.

findings.paper_title: Denbighshire County Council - Audit of Accounts report 2023-24 App 3
findings.headline: The council has chosen not to correct a £262,000 non-current and £14,000 current lease liability for Rhyl Railway Station Buildings, which it plans to correct in 2024-25.
findings.detail: The lease liability had not been recognised on the balance sheet. The paper records this as the only uncorrected misstatement, to be dealt with under the IFRS 16 leasing standard from 2024-25.
findings.matters: An uncorrected misstatement of a lease liability, with its correction tied to the first IFRS 16 year, is a point finance directors here and at other councils will check against their own IFRS 16 transition.
findings.figures: Understatement of non-current liabilities £262,000 and current liabilities £14,000.
findings.quote: We have chosen not to correct this misstatement as the 2024-25 CIPFA Code of Practice will introduce a new leasing standard, IFRS 16.

findings.paper_title: Denbighshire County Council - Audit of Accounts report 2023-24 App 3
findings.headline: Original agreements could not be located for £2.601 million of the £4.085 million of Section 106 commuted sums held at 31 March 2024.
findings.detail: The balances sit within Capital Grants Received in Advance. The council says it has not been possible during the audit window to review all schemes and locate the legal agreements, and Internal Audit is scheduled to review Section 106 income during 2026-27.
findings.matters: Developer contributions held as liabilities are a balance sheet item that depends on conditions and timeframes in legal agreements, and the same issue is likely to affect other councils holding Section 106 balances.

findings.matters: Finance officers elsewhere can compare how a council closed a gap in a year of higher grant funding, and what it plans once that funding stops rising.
findings.figures: £3m of measures to set a balanced budget in 2026/27; £25m of cumulative measures across 2023/24 to 2026/27
findings.quote: Given the increase in funding from Welsh Government it was possible to balance the 2026/27 budget without proposals that were categorised as reductions to service delivery

findings.headline: Council Fund balance increased to £7.6m during 2025/26
findings.detail: The Council agreed a minimum unearmarked reserve of £6.6m for 2026/27 and says a call on the reserve would require a plan to replenish it. The paper also says it aims to keep increasing unearmarked reserves over the medium term where possible.
findings.matters: Rebuilding the unearmarked general reserve gives the council more capacity to absorb unforeseen pressures, which matters to peers and lenders assessing resilience.
findings.figures: £7.6m Council Fund balance; £7.6m is 2.45% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget of £309m; minimum unearmarked reserve agreed at £6.6m
findings.quote: The Council Fund balance was increased during 2025/26 to £7.6m.

findings.headline: Combined school reserves moved from £0.6m to £(2.5)m at the 2025/26 year end, and schools in financial deficit rose from 22 to 25
findings.detail: The paper says the Council is increasingly concerned about school finances, the number of schools in deficit and the rate at which school reserves are falling. Schools' combined use of reserves was £3.1m in 2025/26, and the Council is working with schools and Welsh Government on the position.
findings.matters: A council's schools budget is its largest, and a sector-wide move into negative school reserves is a liability that can return to the council's own balance sheet and budget.
findings.figures: Combined school reserves £0.6m (2024/25 year end) and £(2.5)m (2025/26 year end); schools in financial deficit 22 (2024/25) and 25 (2025/26); combined use of reserves £3.1m in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council is increasingly concerned about the pressure on school finances, the increasing number of schools in financial deficit and the rate at which school reserves are reducing.

findings.headline: The letter of representation for the 2023-24 accounts refers to a qualified audit opinion, excepting the reported issues from its statement that the financial statements are free of material misstatements.
findings.detail: Management's representation that the statements are free of material misstatement is made 'with the exception of the issues reported in the qualified audit opinion'. The paper does not describe the qualification's content, and the qualified opinion itself is not included in this document.
findings.matters: A qualified opinion on a council's accounts is a signal a finance director or lender would track, and this paper confirms the 2023-24 opinion was qualified.
findings.quote: With the exception of the issues reported in the qualified audit opinion, the financial statements are free of material misstatements, including omissions.

findings.headline: The 2023-24 accounts carry an uncorrected omitted lease for Rhyl Railway Station, understating current liabilities by £14,000 and non-current liabilities by £262,000.
findings.detail: The council chose not to correct the misstatement, stating that the 2024-25 CIPFA Code will introduce IFRS 16 and that the lease will be corrected in 2024-25 as part of that work. Management describes the uncorrected misstatements as immaterial, both individually and in aggregate.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would want to know that a lease was left off the balance sheet and deferred to the IFRS 16 transition, as this is a transition issue other councils will also face.
findings.figures: £14,000 understatement of current liabilities; £262,000 understatement of non-current liabilities
findings.quote: Omitted lease liability for Rhyl Railway Station, resulting in an understatement of current liabilities of £14,000 and non-current liabilities of £262,000.

findings.headline: The Council will report to the committee on progress in March 2027, with a timetable to follow for 2024/25 to 2026/27 accounts
findings.detail: The paper says an action plan will be drawn up after the 2023/24 audit concludes, covering issues from both the 2022/23 and 2023/24 audits. It says a more precise timescale for the 2024/25 draft accounts and a timetable for 2025/26 and 2026/27 will be set once the audit is complete.
findings.matters: Committing to a dated progress report and a timetable gives a measurable point at which the Council can show whether its backlog of unaudited accounts is being cleared.
findings.figures: Progress report scheduled for March 2027.
findings.quote: A report to keep the Committee updated with progress is scheduled for March 2027.

findings.headline: The Council's external support contract with CIPFA ended in early 2026, when the two officers working on the project left CIPFA
findings.detail: The paper says CIPFA was engaged on a consultancy basis in July 2025 to complete the required asset register work. That engagement ended at the start of 2026 when the two officers working on the project both left CIPFA.
findings.matters: Losing the external consultancy support midway through the asset register work explains part of the delay, and a finance director considering similar external help would want to see that risk.
findings.figures: CIPFA engaged July 2025; engagement ended at the beginning of 2026.
findings.quote: which ended at the beginning of this calendar year 2026 when the 2 officers who were working on the project both left CIPFA.

findings.headline: The Finance Team has recruited to an additional Accountant post, with the appointee starting in October 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the post was created to address the number of years of accounts still outstanding. It says the new post-holder started in October 2026, and that work on the asset registers will restart once the 2023/24 audit concludes.
findings.matters: Adding capacity to the finance team is the Council's stated route to clearing its backlog, and other councils facing similar delays will want to see whether the added resource delivers.
findings.figures: One additional Accountant post.
findings.quote: The Finance Team have successfully recruited to the additional Accountant post

findings.headline: The Council's 2022/23 Statement of Accounts was approved in July 2026, and the 2023/24 audit is substantially complete
findings.detail: The paper says the 2023/24 audit started in November 2025 and is 'substantially complete', though it continues until the Auditor General signs off. It sets out that the delays on the 2022/23 accounts have had a knock-on effect on later years, and that the draft accounts were produced and reported in July 2025.
findings.matters: A council with multiple years of accounts open can struggle to produce and audit later years, so the timing of sign-off is the key test of whether the backlog is being cleared.
findings.figures: 2022/23 accounts approved July 2026; 2023/24 audit commenced November 2025.
findings.quote: the 2022/23 Statement of Accounts (approved in July 2026) and the 2023/24 Statement of Accounts.

findings.headline: Audit Wales' fee for the 2023/24 audit has risen from an indicative £212k to £300k
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to the audit taking longer than planned and being more involved than expected. It notes that these fee increases are a financial consequence of the delayed accounts.
findings.matters: The additional external audit cost, and the reason given for it, shows the financial cost of the accounts delays and is relevant to any council facing similar slippage.
findings.figures: £212k indicative fee; £300k revised fee.
findings.quote: increased fees by Audit Wales which have increased from the indicative fee of £212k to £300k.

findings.headline: Correcting the asset register issue is reported to have no effect on the Council's net assets
findings.detail: The paper says any correction will reduce one unusable reserve and increase the other by the same amount. It concludes there will be no impact on the Council's overall net assets or its financial position, with the impact confined to the resources needed to resolve the issues.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with a similar asset register problem would want to know that the Council reports the correction as a reclassification between unusable reserves rather than a change in net worth.
findings.figures: None given.
findings.quote: Any correction will involve a reduction of one unusable reserve matched with an increase to the other unusable reserve, meaning no impact on the Council’s overall net assets or the financial position of the Council.

findings.headline: The Council has agreed to a qualified audit opinion for 2022/23 and 2023/24, which Audit Wales will issue
findings.detail: The paper says the qualified opinion is because of a misclassification between the revaluation reserve and the capital adjustment account, with both unusable reserves potentially materially misstated. It states the Council had previously sought to avoid a qualification but now sees it as a pragmatic way to move the issue forward and free up finance team capacity.
findings.matters: Accepting a qualified opinion to close out open years is a deliberate choice that a finance director or lender would want to understand when judging the reliability of the Council's reserve balances.
findings.figures: None given.
findings.quote: Agreement was reached on a qualified audit opinion for financial years 2022/23 and 2023/24 being issued by Audit Wales.

findings.detail: The paper says the qualification arises from issues with the Council's asset registers for 'Other Land and Buildings', which relate to historic accounting entries, some dating back to 2007/08. The Council describes the issues as isolated and says they are technical rather than a change to resources available for services.
findings.matters: A qualified opinion on the 2023/24 accounts, linked to asset register errors dating back to 2007/08, is a live audit weakness that other councils with similar asset records and lenders reviewing the Council's governance would track.
findings.figures: None given as a figure in the paper; the restatement values are described only as 'material'.
findings.quote: Audit Wales’ report includes a qualification by limitation due to the issues with the asset registers.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 23092026 0930 Governance and Audit Committee
findings.headline: Audit Wales reports that the Welsh Government has not clearly set out the support available to councils in the event of a Section 114 report, and made five recommendations to the Welsh Government.
findings.detail: The Audit Wales report on Local Government Funding found that the settlement methodology had not been fully and independently reviewed since 2002 and that restricted grants can be confirmed late. findings.matters: Uncertainty over what support a Welsh council would receive if it issued a Section 114 notice bears directly on the risk assessment of every Welsh council's finances.

findings.headline: Social care, homelessness and education services increasingly reliant on Welsh Government grants, often notified after the financial year starts
findings.detail: The paper says grants now fund core statutory services, and that many are annual and notified late. It says ending a grant may not be possible if it funds demand for core services.
findings.matters: Grant-dependent core services carry a funding cliff risk, and this is a point a lender or peer council would check against its own grant exposure.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: services are becoming increasingly reliant on Welsh Government funding in the form of grants to support core services

findings.headline: Denbighshire Leisure Limited forecast to need additional funding in future years
findings.detail: The paper says the leisure company has faced inflation mainly from pay, food and energy, and that its management fee was only increased recently in 2025/26. Future funding is subject to the Subsidy Control Act 2022 limit and will be reviewed in year.
findings.matters: Arm's-length leisure companies with subsidy limits and unfunded pay awards are a pressure many councils share, and a council-side funding decision would affect the MTFP.
findings.figures: Management fee increase in 2025/26 (amount not given)
findings.quote: Forecasts for future years, in light of additional pressures such as pay awards, are that additional funding will be required.

findings.headline: Cefndy Healthcare forecast to have costs above income in 2026/27, with no recurring funding in the MTFP pending a review
findings.detail: The paper says the council's manufacturing subsidiary is forecast to overspend in 2026/27. No recurring funding has been included in the MTFP while a review of its future is ongoing.
findings.matters: A council-owned trading business with a forecast shortfall and no budgeted fix is a contingent liability that other councils with similar companies would want to track.
findings.figures: 2026/27 forecast pressure; no recurring funding in the MTFP
findings.quote: No recurring additional funding has been included within the MTFP pending the conclusion of a review of its future which is ongoing.

findings.headline: Welsh Government AEF assumed to rise 1.5% in 2027/28 and 1% in later years, with no confirmed future levels
findings.detail: The paper says the predictions are a working assumption, since WG gave no indication of future funding levels at the 2026/27 final settlement. It says each 1% of AEF is worth about £2m and that WG's budget is projected to stay broadly flat in real terms.
findings.matters: Each 1% of AEF is a sensitivity figure for any council in Wales, and the paper's assumption sets the core funding line for the MTFP.
findings.figures: 1.5% AEF increase for 2027/28; 1% in future years; c£2m per 1% of AEF
findings.quote: The current predictions for future funding from Welsh Government assume an increase of 1.5% for 2027/28 and 1% in future years in the absence of any other information.

findings.headline: A 5.3% Council Tax rise for 2027/28 would yield £4.7m and address about a third of the funding gap, leaving £8m
findings.detail: The paper's mid-range Council Tax assumption is 5.3% for 2027/28, with a range of 4% to 7% in the MTFP. It says no decisions have been made, and that setting Council Tax at 15% in theory would balance the budget without reductions.
findings.matters: The size of the residual gap after Council Tax is the figure that determines how much a council must cut or fund from reserves, so it is the number finance directors and lenders will compare.
findings.figures: 5.3% mid-range rise; £4.7m additional income; £8m remaining gap; 15% theoretical rise; 4% to 7% range
findings.quote: A mid-range assumption of a Council Tax increase of 5.3% for 2027/28 yields an additional £4.7m and addresses roughly a third of the funding gap, the remaining gap is £8m.

findings.headline: Denbighshire balanced 2026/27 without proposals categorised as reductions to service delivery
findings.detail: The paper says the increase in Welsh Government funding allowed the 2026/27 budget to be balanced through efficiency, income generation and transformation projects instead of service reductions. It adds that the council has not been able to predict the savings needed for later years.
findings.matters: A council that balanced one year through efficiency and income rather than service cuts gives peers a comparison point for how the same pressures were handled.
findings.figures: £3m measures to set a balanced budget in 2026/27; £25m cumulative from 2023/24 to 2026/27
findings.quote: Given the increase in funding from Welsh Government it was possible to balance the 2026/27 budget without proposals that were categorised as reductions to service delivery

findings.headline: Cumulative pressures of £94m over 2023/24 to 2026/27 against £51m of Welsh Government funding, £18m of Council Tax and £25m of savings
findings.detail: The paper's table sets out four years of pressures, funding and savings. It says WG funding has addressed just over half of the pressures, so the council has had to find savings and raise Council Tax.
findings.matters: The four-year table gives a full cumulative picture of how one council has closed a pressure gap, which lets peers compare the mix of funding and savings.
findings.figures: £94m pressures; £51m AEF; £18m Council Tax; £25m measures to set a balanced budget (cumulative, 2023/24 to 2026/27)
findings.quote: The cumulative pressures over the 4-year period from 2023/24 to 2026/27 total £94m.

findings.headline: School reserves stood at -£2.457m at 1 April 2026, with 25 schools in financial deficit in 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper says the council is increasingly concerned about school finances, the number of schools in deficit and the rate at which school reserves are falling. The combined schools reserve moved from a positive £0.6m at 1 April 2025 to a negative £2.457m at 1 April 2026.
findings.matters: A net negative schools reserve is a balance-sheet liability the council must manage, and the trend is the kind of pressure other councils with delegated schools budgets will recognise.
findings.figures: -£2.457m school reserves at 1 April 2026; £0.604m at 1 April 2025; 25 schools in financial deficit in 2025/26; 22 in 2024/25
findings.quote: The Council is increasingly concerned about the pressure on school finances, the increasing number of schools in financial deficit and the rate at which school reserves are reducing.

findings.headline: Council Fund balance rose to £7.6m at 1 April 2026, up from £5.576m a year earlier
findings.detail: The paper says the unearmarked balance was increased during 2025/26, and that £7.6m is 2.45% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget of £309m. It also says the council aims to keep increasing unearmarked reserves over the medium term where possible.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing unearmarked reserves with net budget will see a stated increase in the cover ratio, which is a figure many peers and lenders track.
findings.figures: £7.576m at 1 April 2026; £5.576m at 1 April 2025; 2.45% of £309m net revenue budget
findings.quote: The Council Fund balance was increased during 2025/26 to £7.6m.

findings.headline: The 2028/29 priorities estimate of £250k, Salt Barns at £125k and Archives at £139k are described as high-level estimates, with further work to follow capital bids in autumn 2026.
findings.detail: The paper states that these are high-level estimates and that further work is required after capital bids are considered in autumn 2026. It also notes that the 2029/30 figures are high-level estimates.
findings.matters: Capital items that are not yet costed can move the revenue position, and a finance director would want to see when the estimates are firmed up.
findings.figures: Priorities £250k; Salt Barns £125k; Archives £139k
findings.quote: 28/29 - High-level estimate for priorities (£250k), Salt Barns (£125k) and Archives (£139k)

findings.headline: The paper assumes Revenue Support Grant changes of 1%, 1.5% and 2% in the absence of anything else being available.
findings.detail: The grant assumption is presented as a placeholder rather than a confirmed settlement. The table shows the grant reduction in 2027/28 as £2,299m, £3,449m and £4,598m across the three scenarios.
findings.matters: Grant assumptions drive a large share of the gap, and a council relying on placeholder figures is one peers and lenders would want to compare once settlements are confirmed.
findings.figures: 2027/28 reduction: -£2,299m (low), -£3,449m (medium), -£4,598m (high)
findings.quote: Revenue Support Grant: Assuming 1%, 1.5%, 2% in the absence of anything else being available.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care pressure is put at £3,000m, £3,340m and £4,000m for 2027/28, with detailed calculations completed as at the end of September and to be refined through the autumn.
findings.detail: The paper states that detailed pressure calculations for Adult Social Care were completed at the end of September and will continue to be reviewed as demand changes. Children's Services pressure for 2027/28 is shown as £600m, £1,074m and £2,000m across the same scenarios.
findings.matters: Social care demand pressures are a major component of the gap, and the paper says the figures remain open to change, which a lender or peer would want to track.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care 2027/28: £3,000m (low), £3,340m (medium), £4,000m (high); Children's Services 2027/28: £600m (low), £1,074m (medium), £2,000m (high)
findings.quote: Adult Social Care: Detailed pressure calculations completed as at the end of September, calculations will continue to be reviewed and refined throughout the autumn as demand can change.

findings.headline: Pay grading pressures of £849m in 2027/28 are shown under all three scenarios, following the implementation of the council's new pay structure in April 2026.
findings.detail: The pay grading pressure is the same in each scenario for 2027/28 and falls to £347m for 2028/29 before ending. The paper links the pressure directly to the new pay structure implemented in April 2026.
findings.matters: Pay structure costs are a recurring pressure that other councils implementing new grading structures would want to compare with their own estimates.
findings.figures: 2027/28: £849m (low, medium and high); 2028/29: £347m (low, medium and high)
findings.quote: Pay Grading: Pressures in 27/28 and 28/29 following the implementation of the Council's new pay structure implemented in April 2026

findings.headline: The paper gives council tax increases of 11%, 15% and 20% as the levels required to bridge the total budget gap, on the basis that no savings are achieved.
findings.detail: The paper shows the council tax level needed to close the total gap under each scenario. It notes that these are theoretical figures that assume no savings are achieved. The council tax assumption for 26/27 is 4%, 5% and 7% across the same scenarios.
findings.matters: A finance officer at another council would want to compare how much of a gap is being presented as closable through council tax alone.
findings.figures: 11% (low), 15% (medium), 20% (high); 26/27 assumptions 4% (L), 5% (M), 7% (H)
findings.quote: (theoretical, assumes no savings achieved)

findings.headline: Denbighshire's cumulative budget gap is shown at £5,854m, £7,746m and £10,431m for 2027/28 under low, medium and high scenarios, rising to £18,789m, £27,081m and £36,383m by 2029/30.
findings.detail: The table gives the cumulative gap for each scenario across three years, with the high scenario reaching £36,383m by 2029/30. The table is headed £m throughout, while the notes to it give the priorities and capital items in £k, so the units should be checked against the source.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, would want to compare the scale of the gap and the scenario range against their own medium-term position.

findings.headline: Denbighshire's corporate risk register rates its residual financial sustainability risk as "critical" and records it as outside risk appetite.
findings.detail: Risk 1 (Financial sustainability) has an inherent score of A1 and a residual score of C1, and is owned by the Section 151 Officer. The register says the risk is outside appetite: compliance matters are classed as cautious, so it "should be at most a moderate risk", yet the residual score is "critical". The listed impacts include a "Risk of Section 114 notice".
findings.matters: A finance director here or at another council would note that the council's own top-level financial risk is rated "critical" and outside appetite, with a Section 114 notice named among its impacts.
findings.figures: Residual risk score C1 (Likelihood C: Possible; Impact 1: Very high); inherent risk score A1 (Likelihood A: Almost certain).
findings.quote: However, the residual score for this risk is classed as critical.

findings.headline: Social care safeguarding is scored A1 Critical (Red) at both inherent and residual levels, with systemic social care pressures including high caseloads and recruitment and retention difficulties cited as the cause.
findings.detail: The safeguarding risk is rated Almost Certain and Very High Impact both before and after controls, and is recorded as outside risk appetite. The register links the risk to high caseloads and recruitment and retention difficulties in social care.
findings.matters: Social care demand and staffing pressure are a major cost driver for councils, so a finance officer elsewhere would read this as the same pressure shaping their own budget and workforce costs.
findings.figures: Inherent: A1 Critical (Red), Risk Almost Certain and Very High Impact. Residual: A1 Critical (Red), Risk: Almost Certain and Very High Impact. Within risk appetite: No.
findings.quote: There is a risk that systemic pressures within social care including high caseloads and recruitment and retention difficulties reduce the council's capacity to safeguard vulnerable individuals

findings.headline: Financial sustainability is scored at C1 Critical (Red) residual risk, with likelihood moving from Almost Certain (A1 inherent) to Possible, and is recorded as outside risk appetite.
findings.detail: The register rates the financial sustainability risk at A1 Critical (Red) inherent and C1 Critical (Red) residual, with the residual impact still 'Very High'. The 'Within Risk Appetite' column is marked 'No'. The risk covers demand for services combined with financial and other resource pressures exceeding the council's sustainable capacity to deliver statutory obligations.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, can compare how Denbighshire's own register scores its core financial risk before and after controls, and note that the council still places it outside appetite.
findings.figures: Inherent: A1 Critical (Red), Risk Almost Certain and Very High Impact. Residual: C1 Critical (Red), Risk: Possible and Very High Impact. Within risk appetite: No.
findings.quote: There is a risk that growing and increasingly complex demand for services, alongside financial and other resource pressures, exceeds the council's sustainable capacity to deliver statutory obligations, strategic objectives and effective services for residents.

findings.headline: Denbighshire lists the budget position of schools among emerging risks to be monitored, alongside artificial intelligence and food security.
findings.detail: The paper says these emerging risks are in addition to the 12 corporate risks and will be monitored as they develop. It does not give any figures on school budgets.
findings.matters: A school budget position flagged as an emerging council-wide risk could affect the council's overall financial position, which finance directors and lenders would track.
findings.quote: These include Artificial Intelligence, food security, and the budget position of schools.

findings.headline: Denbighshire has changed its risk appetite for reputation and credibility from 'open' to 'cautious'.
findings.detail: The Risk Appetite Statement change is one of the two recommendations to the committee. The paper does not say what drove the change.
findings.matters: A council that moves its stated appetite toward caution on reputation signals how it will weigh risk-taking in future decisions, which other finance officers and lenders can compare against their own councils.
findings.quote: For matters related to reputation and credibility, the risk appetite has changed from an ‘open’ appetite to a ‘cautious’ one.

findings.headline: Three of the twelve corporate risks are within the council's agreed risk appetite.
findings.detail: Each risk has been categorised against the current Risk Appetite Statement. The paper says the council's approach to risk appetite will be reviewed with its corporate insurers from December 2026.
findings.matters: Nine of twelve risks sitting outside the agreed appetite is a measure of how far the council's current risk exposure runs beyond the level it has said it will accept.
findings.figures: three of twelve corporate risks within appetite; nine outside appetite (derived from the paper's count of twelve risks)
findings.quote: Currently only three of the twelve corporate risks are within the agreed risk appetite.

findings.headline: Denbighshire scores financial sustainability as C1 - Critical on its corporate risk register, after existing controls are considered.
findings.detail: The register's residual scores range from critical to moderate across 12 corporate risks, and none is scored minor. Financial sustainability is the first theme in the table and carries the top residual grade. The paper says six risks are critical and should be a particular consideration.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, would want to know that the council's own risk process rates financial sustainability at the highest residual grade.
findings.figures: Financial sustainability C1 - Critical; six corporate risks scored as critical; 12 corporate risks in total
findings.quote: Financial sustainability C1 - Critical

findings.headline: Denbighshire's corporate risks on financial sustainability and early intervention are rated "Critical (Red)" residual and outside risk appetite
findings.detail: The paper names two corporate risks linked to budget setting: Risk 1, Financial Sustainability, and Risk 2, Early intervention and prevention. It says that despite considerable mitigating activity, both residual scores sit outside the council's risk appetite.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director reads a council's own residual risk rating on financial sustainability as a direct statement of how far it sees its position from its risk appetite.
findings.figures: 2 corporate risks; residual rating "Critical (Red)"
findings.quote: Despite considerable activity being taken to reduce the inherent risks the residual risk score for both is at the Critical (Red) level and outside our risk appetite

findings.headline: Denbighshire assumes 1.5% growth in Welsh Government funding for the medium term, with no future settlement indication
findings.detail: The paper says the 2026/27 settlement gave no indication of future funding. The forecast assumes 1.5% growth in the absence of guidance, which it says is similar to other Welsh councils' assumptions.
findings.matters: Finance officers at other Welsh councils can check whether their own grant assumptions match this working assumption.
findings.figures: 1.5% assumed Welsh Government funding increase; 2026/27 settlement
findings.quote: The 2026/27 funding settlement from Welsh Government provided no future indication of funding.

findings.headline: Denbighshire's 2027/28 budget pressures are forecast at £12m to £21m, with a mid-range of £16m
findings.detail: The paper says pressures are difficult to forecast and similar ranges are expected for 2028/29 and 2029/30. It attributes the pressures to demand and complexity in Education, Social Care and Homelessness.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere can compare the scale of pressure in statutory services against their own forecast ranges.
findings.figures: £12m low; £21m high; £16m mid-range; 2027/28
findings.quote: Pressures are difficult to forecast but are ranging from £12m to £21m in 2027/28 with a mid-range of £16m.

findings.headline: Denbighshire forecasts a 2027/28 to 2029/30 budget gap of £19m to £36m, with a mid-range of £27m
findings.detail: The paper gives a three-year forecast gap with a low, high and mid-range projection. The range is wide, and the paper says the figures are uncertain and that further work is needed to refine them.
findings.matters: The size of the three-year gap, and how wide its range is, shows the savings a council must still identify over the medium term.
findings.figures: £19m low; £36m high; £27m mid-range; period 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.quote: Over the 3 year period (2027/28 – 2029/30) the forecast gap ranges from a low of £19m to a high of £36m, with a mid-range projection of £27m.

findings.headline: Denbighshire's remaining 2027/28 budget gap after a 5% council tax rise is £8m, down from the May forecast
findings.detail: The paper says a mid-range 5% council tax increase for 2027/28 yields £4.7m, which addresses about a third of the gap. The remaining gap is £8m, which the paper says has come down from its May forecast.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how much of a gap council tax covers against the residual that must come from savings or reserves.
findings.figures: £4.7m additional revenue from a 5% council tax increase in 2027/28; remaining gap £8m; 5% council tax assumption
findings.quote: The remaining gap is substantial at £8m, though that has come down from the last forecast in May of this year.

findings.headline: Sole cashable benefit identified is licensing savings, "a small saving", realised after implementation and a transitionary period
findings.detail: The sole cashable benefit identified is savings on existing software licensing from moving to a hosted solution on mainstream technology. However, the amount is not quantified (described only as 'a small saving'), and these savings will only be realised after implementation and a transitionary period. The council must fund the full cost of both systems during transition before any offsetting benefit arrives.
findings.matters: A council is committing significant capital and revenue with only one financial benefit and that benefit is unquantified, described as small, and delayed, creating a prolonged period where the investment has no offsetting return to the budget.
findings.figures: Licensing savings described as 'a small saving'; timing post-implementation and transitionary period; amounts not specified
findings.quote: will allow us to make a small saving on licensing we currently have in place to cover the incumbent system's infrastructure

findings.headline: Implementation delay beyond August 2028 would trigger renegotiation of incumbent supplier contract at higher cost
findings.detail: The council's existing support contract for the current system (Open Housing) has a fixed extension deadline of 31 March 2028. The council targets decommissioning by 31 August 2028, creating a 5-month window. If this target is missed, the council would need to renegotiate a further extension with the supplier at terms the supplier proposes.
findings.matters: Project schedule slippage creates unbudgeted cost risk: missing the decommissioning deadline would force the council to renegotiate supplier contract terms at potentially significantly higher cost.
findings.figures: Current contract extension deadline 31 March 2028; decommissioning target 31 August 2028; 5-month contingency window
findings.quote: Should we not be able to decommission the system by 31/08/2028, we face having to reach an agreement to extend the support. It is likely that any further extension would see a potential significant increase in cost and may also require us to upgrade the system again.

findings.headline: Cost-benefit analysis incomplete and full project costs not disclosed in business case
findings.detail: The council's cost-benefit analysis is still under development and will be refined through several iterations. The business case references draft costs in Appendix 3 but this appendix is not included in the published version (marked as Part 2 confidential information). Full costs will only emerge when suppliers submit tender responses.
findings.matters: A council is advancing a major capital procurement without having completed its own cost-benefit analysis or disclosing project costs, raising questions about financial planning and decision-making.
findings.figures: Draft costs in Appendix 3 (not disclosed); full costs to be determined at tender evaluation stage; revenue costs for first 7-year term to be included in supplier pricing
findings.quote: The cost benefit analysis is still currently being developed. Given the uncertainty of the outcome of the procurement process, this is a complex process and will develop over several iterations of this Business Case.

findings.headline: Council committing to multi-year capital and revenue expenditure with no immediate cashable benefits
findings.detail: The council is committing to significant capital costs for implementation plus ongoing annual revenue costs for a replacement housing management system over a 7-year initial contract term, extendable annually. The business case explicitly states there are no immediate cashable benefits, with only non-cashable benefits and software licensing savings to be realised only after implementation and a transitionary period.
findings.matters: A council is making a major multi-year financial commitment with material revenue budget implications but no offsetting financial returns in the short to medium term.
findings.figures: Initial contract period 7 years with annual extension options to maximum 21 years; support contract for existing system expires 31 March 2027 with 12-month extension option to 31 March 2028
findings.quote: There are no immediate cashable benefits arising from the business case. However, following implementation and a transitionary period, savings on existing software licensing will be realised

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Temporary borrowing from other councils reduced to £10m from £19m year-on-year
findings.detail: The council's reliance on short-term borrowing to manage cash flow decreased significantly during the year. This reduction of £9m represents a 47% decrease in temporary borrowing compared to the prior year end, suggesting improved cash flow management and reduced need for temporary funding solutions.
findings.matters: Reduction in short-term borrowing indicates improved liquidity and working capital management, reducing near-term refinancing risks.
findings.figures: Temporary borrowing £10m at 31 March 2026 vs £19m at 31 March 2025; reduction of £9m or 47.4%
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council had £10m in temporary loans from one local authority, compared to £19m at the previous year end 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council confirmed no breaches of prudential indicators for 2025-26 and reports adoption of prudent treasury approach
findings.detail: The council's treasury activity operated within all mandatory prudential limits during the year. Borrowing remained below the Capital Financing Requirement (£336.97m actual vs £400.87m CFR), fixed rate exposure was 97.04% against a 100% limit, and peak external borrowing reached £349.3m within the authorised limit of £430m.
findings.matters: Prudential compliance demonstrates the council's borrowing decisions remain affordable and sustainable within regulatory limits despite increased debt and capital activity.
findings.figures: External borrowing £336,971k vs CFR £400,871k; peak borrowing £349.3m vs authorised limit £430m; fixed rate exposure 97.04% vs upper limit 100%
findings.quote: None of the Prudential Indicators have been breached and a prudent approach has been taken in relation to investment activity with priority being given to security and liquidity over yield.

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Financing cost ratio for Non-HRA improved to 5.96% from estimated 7.52%; HRA ratio improved to 37.19% from estimated 44.46%
findings.detail: Despite increased borrowing during the year, the proportion of revenue budget required to meet borrowing costs came in significantly lower than estimated for both non-HRA and HRA. Non-HRA financing costs were £17.402m against estimated £20.535m, while HRA financing costs were £7.668m against estimated £7.407m. The council notes the overall revenue overspend was separately reported to Cabinet.
findings.matters: Better-than-expected debt service ratios suggest actual affordability is stronger than forecast, either due to conservative estimates or capital spending phasing improvements.
findings.figures: Non-HRA: 5.96% actual vs 7.52% estimated; HRA: 37.19% actual vs 44.46% estimated; Non-HRA financing costs £17.402m vs £20.535m estimate; HRA financing costs £7.668m vs £7.407m estimate
findings.quote: The overall revenue overspend compared to budget has been separately reported to Cabinet (30 June 2026) with reasons provided for the overspend.

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Non-HRA capital expenditure outturn of £55.75m exceeded January 2025 estimate of £48.16m by £7.58m
findings.detail: The council's capital spending on non-housing services ran significantly above its estimate. The council attributes this to additional schemes being approved and additional funding being awarded after the estimate was set in January 2025. The HRA capital programme came in under estimate at £13.67m against £16.04m estimate.
findings.matters: Capital overspends can signal accelerated spending, scope creep, or increased capital commitments that affect future debt service and spending plans.
findings.figures: Non-HRA: £55,747k actual vs £48,163k estimate (£7.584m or 15.8% overspend); HRA: £13,674k actual vs £16,040k estimate; Total: £69,421k actual vs £64,203k estimate
findings.quote: The outturn non-HRA capital spend for 2025/26 is higher than the original estimate due to additional schemes being approved and additional funding (grants etc) being awarded after January 2025.

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's total external borrowing increased to £326.97m at 31 March 2026 with average debt rate rising from 4.49% to 4.86%
findings.detail: The council borrowed £65m in new funding during the year (£20m from PWLB and £45m from NWF) while repaying £43.454m in maturing loans. As a result of this net increase in borrowing, the average rate on the council's debt rose by 37 basis points, reflecting higher borrowing costs in the current interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Rising cost of debt service is a key affordability indicator for lenders assessing whether the council can service increased debt levels without revenue stress.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £305,425k (1 April 2025) → £326,971k (31 March 2026); average rate 4.49% → 4.86%; new borrowing £65,000k; maturing loans £43,454k
findings.quote: As a result of this borrowing, the average rate on the Council's debt increased slightly from 4.49% at 1 April 2025 to 4.86% at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Reduction in employers pension contributions of £1,604k achieved through triennial pension fund review, representing 87.8% of total achieved savings
findings.detail: The council achieved £1,604k from reduced employers pension contributions following the pension fund triennial review, marked as fully achieved. This single item accounts for £1,604k of the £1,820k total achieved savings.
findings.matters: A large one-off pension gain masks the underlying delivery rate of operational savings plans; the council's 57.4% achievement rate is heavily dependent on non-recurring pension fund benefit
findings.figures: £1,604k achieved; represents 87.8% of total £1,820k achieved savings
findings.quote: Reduction in employers pension contributions as a result of triennial review of pension fund Other 1,604 Achieved 1,604 0

findings.headline: Homelessness service reform not achieved; £100k shortfall on planned prevention and accommodation redesign
findings.detail: The transformation initiative to reform homelessness services by focusing on prevention and moving from temporary accommodation (hotels and B&Bs) to leased private sector accommodation is marked 'Not Achieved' with £100k shortfall.
findings.matters: Undelivered homelessness reform leaves the council committed to continuing high-cost temporary accommodation spending, indicating underlying demand pressure not being addressed
findings.figures: £100k shortfall
findings.quote: Reforming the model for delivering homelessness services. Focus on prevention and moving away from temporary emergency accommodation through use of hotels and B&Bs.

findings.headline: In-house residential care homes for children not achieved; full £548k shortfall after planned September 2026 opening
findings.detail: The scheme to develop small care homes for children in-house, intended to open in September 2026, is marked 'Not Achieved' with zero current-year savings and the full £548k shortfall. This was a transformation initiative aimed at reducing reliance on independent agencies.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver major transformation schemes suggests execution or capacity constraints that affect the council's ability to reshape service delivery and reduce long-term cost exposure
findings.figures: £548k shortfall on £548k proposal
findings.quote: In house residential provision through the development of small care homes for children. Plan to open first in Sept 2026.

findings.headline: Savings proposals tracking £738k shortfall against £3.17m 2026/27 target, with 20.4% of proposals not achieved

findings.paper_title: App 2 - Denbighshire CC Final Audit of Accounts Report 2022-23
findings.headline: Audit encountered significant difficulties reconciling transaction populations; financial ledger structure required manual combination of multiple reports
findings.detail: The audit team encountered significant difficulties reconciling populations for employee benefit expenses, fees and charges income, and other service expenditure. The financial ledger structure did not allow a single auditable population to be formed, requiring many reports to be generated and manually combined, consuming considerable time from both audit and finance staff.
findings.matters: This indicates fundamental weaknesses in the council's financial ledger and reporting controls, making it difficult to verify the accuracy and completeness of financial statements. It suggests the finance function lacks robust systems for transaction classification and reporting.
findings.figures: Not quantified, but described as requiring 'considerable amount of time' from both audit and finance teams
findings.quote: During the audit, the audit team encountered significant difficulties in reconciling populations for several classes of transaction including employee benefit expenses, fees, charges and other service income and other service expenditure. The structure of the financial ledger did not allow for a single population to be formed for the transaction lines within Note 5 to the financial statements. Many reports had to be generated from the ledger and combined, to create one transaction level population that was auditable.

findings.paper_title: App 2 - Denbighshire CC Final Audit of Accounts Report 2022-23
findings.headline: Material asset disposal not accounted for until two years after the event
findings.detail: An asset disposed of in the 2020-21 financial year was not accounted for by the council until 2022-23, requiring a £12.865 million correction across multiple years. This multi-year latency indicates weak asset disposal controls and reconciliation processes.
findings.matters: The delayed recognition of a major asset disposal suggests poor controls over fixed asset accounting and the completeness of financial records, both critical to lenders assessing financial management quality.
findings.figures: £12,865,000 adjustment for prior-year asset disposal; affected both 2021-22 and 2022-23 accounts

findings.paper_title: App 2 - Denbighshire CC Final Audit of Accounts Report 2022-23
findings.headline: Audit completion massively delayed: 20 months overdue from original November 2023 deadline
findings.detail: The audit report, dated July 2026, was originally due in November 2023. The delay has been driven by significant accounting problems requiring extensive investigation, including complex capital accounting issues, difficulties reconciling transaction populations, and issues with valuations and asset disposals that took considerable audit team time to resolve.
findings.matters: A 20-month audit delay signals either severe accounting control problems or an unmanageable finance function, both of which concern lenders. It prevents timely financial reporting and delays stakeholder access to verified accounts. The council's inability to maintain clean, reconcilable records suggests systemic control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Original deadline: November 2023; Actual issue date: July 2026

findings.paper_title: App 2 - Denbighshire CC Final Audit of Accounts Report 2022-23
findings.headline: Qualified audit opinion issued due to unquantified errors in asset valuations and revaluation reserves
findings.detail: The auditor has issued a qualified (rather than clean) opinion on the accounts because the council has incompletely and incorrectly recorded historical cost asset information and revaluation movements that cannot be quantified. The errors may date back to 2007-08 and affect both the revaluation reserve (£226.6m) and capital adjustment account (£233.3m). The council has been unable to determine the full value of the misstatement despite attempting a full review of asset movements since 2007-08.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion is a material red flag to lenders about the reliability of the council's financial statements and the effectiveness of its controls. The fact that systematic errors dating back 16 years remain unresolved indicates fundamental weaknesses in asset accounting governance.
findings.figures: Revaluation reserve £226,614,000; Capital adjustment account £233,316,000; uncorrected difference between fixed asset register and financial ledger of £8.9 million as at 31 March 2023
findings.quote: Due to incomplete historical information, it has not been possible to determine when these issues first arose. However, they may date back to 2007-08, when the Revaluation Reserve was introduced by the Code of Practice on Local Authority Accounting in the United Kingdom. The Council is currently analysing its accounting records to correct for this matter but to date has been unable to quantify the full value of the misstatement.

findings.headline: Statutory service cost pressures growing faster than available funding

The council is setting aside additional reserves to address these pressures, signalling they expect continued strain.
findings.matters: Statutory services (social care and education) must be funded. If costs are growing faster than funding and cannot be constrained, the council faces structural budget pressure that will require further savings or reserve depletion in coming years.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection shortfall of £939k from rising historic debt

findings.matters: Historic debt buildup indicates weakening collection performance and cash flow pressure. The pattern is not council-specific but systemic across Wales, suggesting potential structural issues in council finances across the region.
findings.figures: £939k shortfall, in-year collection 96.88% (3rd highest in Wales)

findings.matters: School deficits are a leading indicator of broader pressure on education budgets; the reversal is positive but the speed and magnitude raises questions about sustainability and whether primary budget pressure merely shifted to the council's account

findings.headline: Council's unearmarked reserves stand at only 2.14% of the net revenue budget, limiting shock absorption
findings.detail: The Council Fund balance is £6.6m, which represents 2.14% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget of £309m. findings.headline: Children's placements and homelessness costs are rising faster than inflation and are difficult to control
findings.detail: The council identifies Children's Services placements as having demand that is "difficult to forecast" with "complexity of needs coupled with inflation" driving up costs significantly. Welsh Government's priority to eliminate private profit from looked-after children's care is driving costs up in advance of legislative deadlines. For homelessness, a "significant increase in the number of people presenting as homeless in recent years" has led to "significant additional cost, particularly in relation to temporary accommodation." While workstreams aim to reduce costs, "the situation can change quickly."
findings.matters: These are statutory services where demand and cost pressures are largely outside the council's control. Unbudgeted cost escalation in these areas would directly impact the council's ability to balance budgets and would require draw-down of reserves or cuts to other services.
findings.figures: No specific quantum given; identified as an emerging risk with the caveat that homelessness temporary accommodation costs are "significant" and that workstreams show "positive results to reduce the costs"

WG have set a priority of eliminating private profit from the care of looked after children, this is having an impact on the market in Wales by driving up costs in advance of those legislative deadlines.

findings.headline: An £11m funding gap remains for 2027/28 even with a 5.9% Council Tax rise; 19% increase would be needed to avoid service cuts
findings.detail: For 2027/28, a mid-range Council Tax increase of 5.9% would yield only £5m and address roughly a third of the funding gap, leaving an £11m shortfall. The council would need to raise Council Tax by 19% to balance the budget without service reductions. No indication of Welsh Government funding levels beyond 2026/27 has been provided.
findings.matters: The council faces difficult and politically constrained choices to close a material gap. A lender needs to understand whether the council has credible plans to close the gap and whether reliance on service cuts or reserves will erode financial resilience.
findings.figures: 2027/28 funding gap £11m; Council Tax increase assumption 5.9% yielding £5m; Council Tax increase required to balance without cuts 19%
